analysis.one_liner: Requires employers with 15 or more workers to provide at least seven paid sick days a year.
analysis.headline: The Healthy Families Act drew 66 cosponsors after its June 2004 introduction, but was referred to three committees and never received a hearing or vote before Congress ended in January 2005.
analysis.plain_summary: The bill would have required employers with 15 or more employees to give workers paid sick leave: seven days a year for full-time workers, and a prorated amount for part-timers working at least 20 hours a week or 1,000 hours a year. Workers could use the leave for their own illness, preventive care, or to care for a child, spouse, or parent. The Labor Department would enforce it, and employers could not cut existing leave to comply. It was sent to three House committees, referred to two subcommittees, and died there without any action.
analysis.who_benefits: Workers at employers with 15 or more employees — especially the low-income workers who, according to the bill's findings, most often lack paid sick leave — would gain a guaranteed minimum of paid sick days they could use for themselves or a sick family member, without risking their job or income. Employers that already offer equivalent leave would see no required change.

how_it_helps.text: Employers with 15 or more employees must provide at least 7 days of paid sick leave annually to workers on 30 or more hours a week, and a prorated amount to part-timers working at least 20 hours a week or 1,000 hours a year.
Leave can be used for the employee's own physical or mental illness, injury, or medical care, or to care for a child, spouse, parent, or a person with an equivalent family relationship.
The bill's findings state that 76 percent of the poorest families lack regular sick leave, and that parents unable to miss work send contagious children to school and child care, spreading illness.

Employers are barred from discharging or retaliating against workers who use the leave or file complaints, and the Secretary of Labor gains enforcement authority including employee lawsuits with reinstatement and back pay.
Employers cannot eliminate or reduce existing leave to comply, and the bill does not override state or local laws or collective bargaining agreements that provide more generous leave.

analysis.who_pays: Employers with 15 or more employees bear the cost of paid days off for workers who get sick, plus recordkeeping and compliance costs. Employers that already provide equivalent paid leave are exempt from changing their policies.

drawbacks.text: The mandate is a real cost for covered employers, who must pay wages for time not worked — a burden that falls hardest on low-margin businesses in retail, food service, and care work, where paid sick leave was least common.
The 15-employee threshold means businesses just below it avoid the mandate entirely, and employers must maintain records and a posted notice, with a fine of up to $100 per willful posting violation.

Opponents could reasonably argue the federal minimum should be lower or more flexible for very small firms, and that the bill's medical-certification and notice rules (7 days' advance notice for foreseeable leave, doctor's notes for absences over 3 days) add administrative work.

analysis.benefit_vs_cost: For workers, the benefit is direct: guaranteed paid days off to see a doctor or care for a sick child, which the bill's own findings link to faster recovery, less contagion in schools, and lower emergency care costs. The cost falls on employers as paid time and administration; the bill softens this by exempting firms with equivalent policies, requiring only a quarterly accrual, and allowing the employer to schedule around operations. The main honest objection is that a one-size federal mandate priced leave identically for a 15-person shop and a 15,000-person corporation, though the prorated part-time formula and equivalency exemption narrow that gap.

outcome.mechanism: The bill was introduced in June 2004, sent to three House committees and then two subcommittees, and Congress ended in January 2005 with no hearing, markup, or floor vote ever scheduled.

narrative.text: Rosa DeLauro introduced the Healthy Families Act in the House on June 15, 2004, with 48 original cosponsors listed on the bill.
It was referred to the Committees on Education and the Workforce, Government Reform, and House Administration on the day of introduction.
In July 2004 it was referred to the Subcommittee on Civil Service and Agency Organization and the Subcommittee on Workforce Protections; no further action followed.
The bill finished with 66 cosponsors — 65 Democrats and 1 Independent — and died when the 108th Congress ended on January 3, 2005.

outcome.who_came_out_ahead: Covered employers — especially those in retail, food service, and other low-wage sectors with 15 or more employees — avoided a paid sick leave mandate, because the House committees with jurisdiction never acted on the bill.

for.name: Rosa DeLauro
for.what_they_did: Introduced the Healthy Families Act on June 15, 2004.

for.name: 65 of 205 House Democrats
for.what_they_did: Cosponsored the bill; every cosponsor was a Democrat or the chamber's Independent.

against.name: John Boehner
against.role: Chair, House Education and the Workforce Committee
against.what_they_did: The committee he chaired, the primary panel of jurisdiction, never held a hearing or markup on the bill before Congress ended.

against.name: House Republican leadership
against.role: Majority party controlling the House committee schedule and floor calendar, 108th Congress
against.what_they_did: Referred the bill to three committees and never brought it to the floor.

sides.party_line_note: All 66 cosponsors were Democrats or the chamber's Independent; no Republican signed on, and the bill died in committees controlled by the Republican majority without a hearing or vote.

industries.industry: Covered employers (15+ employees), especially retail, food service, and hospitality
industries.note: These businesses would bear the direct cost of paid sick days for hourly workers, a group where paid leave was least common. Their interest in blocking the mandate ran directly against the workers who would have gained leave.

industries.industry: Large employers with existing generous leave policies
industries.note: The bill exempted employers whose existing policies already offer equivalent leave at the employee's discretion, and barred them from cutting leave to comply — so the compliant majority would face little direct cost while gaining a floor under competitors.
